lustful.e: From Middle English lustful, from Old English lustfull (“desirous, wishful”); equivalent to lust + -ful.

lustrous.x: There was not a cloud on the sky, save a few light vapours that congregated near the moon; but even they were lustrous with her presence.

luxuriant.e: Borrowed from Latin lūxuriāns, present participle of lūxuriō, itself from lūxuria (“luxury, excess”). Equivalent to luxury + -ant.
luxuriant.x: Thus, to find luxuriant growths of seaweeds unaffected by man, one must go to the Channel Islands where pollution has not taken its toll.

luxurious.e: From Middle English luxurious, from Old French luxurios (modern French luxurieux), from Latin lū̆xuriōsus (“rank, luxuriant, profuse, excessive, immoderate”), from…

lycanthropy.e: Borrowed from Ancient Greek λῠκᾰνθρωπῐ́ᾱ (lŭkănthrōpĭ́ā), from λῠκᾰ́νθρωπος (lŭkắnthrōpos, “wolfman”). By surface analysis, lycanthrope + -y (abstract noun suffix).

lychee.e: /ˈlaɪ̯.t͡ʃi/, /laɪ̯ˈt͡ʃiː/ from Cantonese 荔枝 (lai⁶ zi¹) * /ˈlit͡ʃi/ from Hokkien 荔枝 (lē-chi) Doublet of litchi and lichi.

lymph.e: Borrowing from French lymphe and/or Latin lympha (“clear water”), from Ancient Greek νῠ́μφη (nŭ́mphē, “bride; spring water”). Doublet of nymph.
lymph.x: She lay face-down, an infected puncture point on the inside of her thigh oozing a faint lymph.

lymphoma.e: From lymph, from Latin lympha (“water”) + -oma (“disease, morbidity”).

lynch.e: First attested 1835, from Lynch law, which appeared in 1811. There is a popular claim that it was named after William Lynch, but equally strong arguments would have it…
lynch.x: I telephoned Bill Brandon in Oxford and begged him to get the new refrigeration unit into production before I got lynched.

lynching.x: The police with difficulty prevented the swaying mass from lynching him on the spot.

lyrics.x: The song’s lyrics were full of nostalgia.
